usage_notes: Use lightly and only when it preserves the anchor meaning and plausible student voice.
safety_notes: Do not make the student sound less intelligent or less educated.
source_references: Labov, Ash, and Boberg (2006), Atlas of North American English
Montgomery and Hall, Dictionary of Smoky Mountain English; modal stacking discussions overlap Southern/Appalachian varieties

usage_notes: Prefer lexical/discourse substitutions because many North Central features are phonological and hard to represent safely in writing.
safety_notes: Avoid turning regional features into parody.
source_references: Labov, Ash, and Boberg (2006), Atlas of North American English
University of Wisconsin DARE resources on regional American vocabulary

disallowed_features: non-rhotic accent spellings like pahk the cah
usage_notes: Prefer lexical items and intensifiers; avoid phonetic spelling of accent features.
safety_notes: Do not represent accent through mocking spellings.
source_references: Labov, Ash, and Boberg (2006), Atlas of North American English
Kurath (1949), A Word Geography of the Eastern United States

usage_notes: Use only subtle lexical or discourse features; many Western features are vowel-system features not suitable for written anchors.
safety_notes: Avoid making the response sound unserious or less capable.
source_references: Labov, Ash, and Boberg (2006), Atlas of North American English
Stanford Voices of California project resources

allowed_syntactic_features: double modals such as might could
usage_notes: Apply grammatical features sparingly and only where they preserve exact meaning.
safety_notes: Do not signal social class or intelligence through the rewrite.
source_references: Montgomery and Hall, Dictionary of Smoky Mountain English
Appalachian English Archive, University of South Carolina

allowed_syntactic_features: stressed BIN for remote past where meaning requires it
disallowed_features: features not licensed by the inventory
usage_notes: Use AAVE grammatical features only where their meaning is appropriate; habitual be must mark habitual aspect, not replace every form of is or are.
safety_notes: Do not make the response sound less intelligent, less academic, or stereotyped.
source_references: Green (2002), African American English: A Linguistic Introduction
Spears (2020), updated list of AAE grammatical features
